Tailwind CSS Hero Section: Free Examples & Code 2026
====================================================

The hero section is the first thing visitors see. A well-crafted Tailwind CSS hero section can make the difference between a visitor staying or leaving. In this guide, we cover every hero section type, the key elements that convert, and provide free copy-paste Tailwind CSS hero section code for HTML and JSX.

1.  [What Is a Hero Section?](https://www.tailwindready.com/blog/tailwind-css-hero-section#what-is)

8.  [Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.tailwindready.com/blog/tailwind-css-hero-section#faq)
    

What Is a Hero Section?
-----------------------

A hero section (also called a "hero banner" or "above-the-fold section") is the large, prominent area at the top of a webpage that a visitor sees before scrolling. It is the first chance to communicate your value proposition, capture attention, and direct the user toward a primary action.

In Tailwind CSS, a hero section is built using utility classes for layout (flexbox or grid), typography (headline and subtext), spacing (padding and margin), and visual design (backgrounds, gradients, shadows). No custom CSS required.

A Tailwind CSS hero section typically takes up 60–100% of the viewport height (`min-h-screen` or a fixed `py-32`) and contains a headline, subtext, one or two CTA buttons, and optionally an image or illustration.

6 Types of Tailwind CSS Hero Sections
-------------------------------------

Different businesses and content types call for different hero layouts. Here are the six most effective Tailwind CSS hero section patterns:

1

### Centered Hero

Best for: SaaS homepages, product launches

A centered layout with headline, subtext, and one or two CTA buttons. The most common hero pattern for SaaS and startup landing pages.

2

### Split Hero

Best for: App showcases, portfolios

Left side text content, right side image or illustration. Great for showcasing a product screenshot alongside a value proposition.

3

### Full-Bleed Hero

Best for: Photography, agencies, editorial

Edge-to-edge background image or video with overlaid text. Best for visually striking brands where imagery is central to the message.

4

### Gradient Hero

Best for: Tech products, crypto, Web3

Bold gradient background (often cyan-to-purple or dark-to-light) with white text. Adds energy and modernity without needing images.

5

### Minimal Hero

Best for: Blogs, portfolios, agencies

Clean white or light background, large typography, minimal decoration. Lets the headline speak for itself.

6

### Video Background Hero

Best for: Events, real estate, hospitality

Looping background video with overlay. Creates immersive first impressions when a static image is not enough.

Key Elements of a High-Converting Hero Section
----------------------------------------------

A beautiful Tailwind CSS hero section is not enough on its own. These six elements, when combined correctly, maximize conversions and reduce bounce rate:

### Pre-headline badge

A small pill or tag above the headline (e.g., 'New', 'Free', 'v2.0 Released'). Draws attention and adds context.

`inline-flex items-center px-3 py-1 rounded-full text-sm bg-cyan-50 text-cyan-700 border border-cyan-200`

### H1 Headline

The most important element. Should be large (text-4xl to text-7xl), bold, and clearly state the value proposition in 5–12 words.

`text-5xl md:text-7xl font-extrabold leading-tight text-gray-900`

### Subheadline / Description

1–2 sentences expanding on the headline. Max 25 words for best readability. Use text-xl or text-2xl.

`text-xl text-gray-600 max-w-2xl leading-relaxed`

### CTA Buttons

Primary CTA (solid, high contrast) + optional secondary CTA (outlined or ghost). Keep button copy action-oriented.

`flex gap-4 items-center flex-wrap`

### Social Proof

Star ratings, user count ('Trusted by 10,000+ developers'), or company logos. Placed below CTAs to reduce friction.

`flex items-center gap-2 text-sm text-gray-500`

### Hero Image / Illustration

Product screenshot, device mockup, or abstract illustration. Visible above the fold on desktop, often hidden on mobile.

`rounded-2xl shadow-2xl border border-gray-200 overflow-hidden`

Making Tailwind CSS Hero Sections Responsive
--------------------------------------------

All hero sections from Tailwindready are mobile-first and fully responsive. Here are the key responsive patterns we use:

Stack on mobile, side-by-side on desktop

`grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 gap-8`

Split heroes collapse to a single column on mobile. The image typically moves below the text.

Adjust font size at breakpoints

`text-3xl md:text-5xl lg:text-7xl`

Large display headlines need to scale down on small screens. Use responsive font size prefixes.

Control padding at breakpoints

`py-16 md:py-24 lg:py-32`

Reduce vertical padding on mobile so the hero doesn't take too much vertical space.

Hide decorative elements on mobile

`hidden md:block`

Background patterns, floating elements, and decorative images are often hidden on small screens.

Hero Section SEO Best Practices
-------------------------------

The hero section is prime SEO real estate. Follow these rules:

*   ✓Always place your primary keyword in the H1 tag within the hero section — it is the first H1 on the page.
*   ✓Keep the H1 headline between 30 and 70 characters for best display in search results.
*   ✓Add alt text to any hero images — describe the image and include a relevant keyword where natural.
*   ✓Avoid hero sliders/carousels with auto-advancing slides — they harm Core Web Vitals (CLS).
*   ✓Use a real background color or CSS gradient instead of a large background image where possible — faster LCP (Largest Contentful Paint).
*   ✓If using a background image, preload it in the <head> with a <link rel='preload'> tag to improve LCP.

Design Tips for Better Tailwind CSS Hero Sections
-------------------------------------------------

One primary CTA, one secondary

Two CTAs of equal visual weight creates decision paralysis. Make the primary CTA solid and prominent, secondary outlined or ghost.

Contrast is conversion

Your CTA button must contrast with the background. Use Tailwind's color scale to ensure at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for accessibility.

Headlines should be scannable

Visitors scan before they read. Use a bold, short headline (5–12 words) that communicates the core value in seconds.

Limit animations

Subtle fade-in or slide-up animations (using Tailwind's transition and animate utilities) can add polish. Avoid anything that delays content visibility.

Test at multiple viewport widths

Always check your hero at 375px (iPhone SE), 768px (tablet), and 1440px (desktop) before shipping.

Use real copy, not Lorem Ipsum

Placeholder text in a hero section makes it impossible to judge the real design. Write real or near-final copy before evaluating the layout.

Frequently Asked Questions
--------------------------

### What height should a Tailwind CSS hero section be?

There is no fixed rule. Full-viewport heroes (min-h-screen) work well for single-page apps and bold brands. For content-heavy sites, a fixed padding (py-24 or py-32) is often better as it doesn't hide page content below the fold.

### How do I add a background pattern to a Tailwind CSS hero?

Use an SVG background pattern as a data URI in a custom CSS class, or use a gradient overlay on top of a texture image. Tailwind's bg-\[url('/pattern.svg')\] arbitrary value syntax works for custom images.

### Can I animate a Tailwind CSS hero section?

Yes. Tailwind includes transition, animate-pulse, animate-bounce, and animate-spin utilities. For custom enter animations, use Tailwind's @keyframes via tailwind.config or a library like Framer Motion with React.

### What is the best font size for a hero headline in Tailwind?

On desktop, text-5xl to text-7xl (48px–72px) is standard for hero headlines. On mobile, scale down to text-3xl or text-4xl (30px–36px) using responsive prefixes like md:text-6xl.

### How do I center content vertically in a Tailwind CSS hero?

Use flex flex-col justify-center min-h-\[80vh\] on the hero container, or use grid place-items-center min-h-screen.

Featuring 132 ready-to-use feature blocks from SERP Blocks for React and Next.js. SB SERP Blocks Team Product Mar 20, 2026 ![Tailwind CSS Feature Section Designs: 100+ Examples cover](https://blocks.serp.co/images/feature.png) Feature sections are the backbone of every marketing page, product landing page, and SaaS homepage. They sit between the hero and the pricing table, and their job is straightforward: explain what your product does, why it matters, and why the visitor should care. A well-designed feature section converts curiosity into understanding. A poorly designed one gets scrolled past without a second glance. Tailwind CSS has become the dominant approach for building feature sections because utility classes let you experiment with layouts, spacing, and responsive behavior directly in your markup. You do not need to maintain a separate stylesheet. You do not need to name things. You prototype a bento grid, decide it does not work, and restructure to an alternating layout — all without leaving your template file. This guide covers every major feature section design pattern in Tailwind CSS, explains when each pattern works best, walks through the responsive behavior and visual hierarchy considerations, and references the [SERP Blocks feature collection](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/feature) , which includes 132 feature section blocks built with Tailwind CSS and Shadcn UI. Anatomy of an Effective Feature Section --------------------------------------- Before diving into specific patterns, every feature section needs three foundational elements working together. ### Section Header The section header anchors the entire feature section. It typically includes a small label or eyebrow text ("Features," "Why Choose Us," "How It Works"), a bold headline that frames the features, and optionally a supporting paragraph. In Tailwind, a typical section header looks like this:

Features

Everything you need to ship faster

Built for developers who value speed, quality, and flexibility.

The `max-w-2xl text-center` pattern centers the header and constrains line length for readability. The eyebrow text uses `text-sm font-semibold text-primary` to create a subtle, branded label above the main headline. ### Feature Items Each feature item communicates a single benefit or capability. All 132 blocks are built with Tailwind CSS and Shadcn UI components. They are responsive by default, accessible, and optimized for Next.js and React. Every block is a complete, self-contained section that you can drop into your page and customize with Tailwind utilities and CSS variables. Beyond feature sections, SERP Blocks provides over 1,200 blocks across 50+ categories. Feature sections rarely exist in isolation — they sit alongside [hero sections](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/hero) (81 blocks), [CTA sections](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/cta) (32 blocks), [pricing tables](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/pricing) (21 blocks), [testimonial sections](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/testimonial) (40 blocks), and [footer layouts](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/footer) (21 blocks). Having all of these from a single, consistent design system means your entire page looks cohesive from top to bottom. Sixty blocks are available for free — no account or payment required. The full Pro library is available as an affordable one-time purchase, giving you lifetime access to every block across every category, including [card layouts](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/card) (110 blocks), [contact forms](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/contact) (33 blocks), [about sections](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/about) (32 blocks), [blog list pages](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/blog-list) (27 blocks), [product pages](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/product) (25 blocks), [gallery components](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/gallery) (25 blocks), and many more. Start with the icon grid pattern if you are unsure which layout to use. It works for nearly every product and scales cleanly across breakpoints. Move to bento grids when you have clear feature hierarchy. Use alternating layouts when you have screenshots to show. Use tabbed sections when each feature needs dedicated screen space. Keep your Tailwind classes consistent across all feature items. Use CSS variables for color theming so you can adjust the entire section's palette from one file. Maintain generous spacing. Prioritize scannability over density. Feature sections are iterative. Build one, measure engagement (scroll depth, CTA clicks), and refine the design. ![SERP UI logo](https://imagedelivery.net/Kpcbofvpelk1jdjXmWIr5w/3932163b-825d-4a66-22d7-a64cd0ed1300/public) [SERPUI](https://blocks.serp.co/) * [Blocks](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks) * Categories * [Pricing](https://blocks.serp.co/pricing) * [Docs](https://blocks.serp.co/docs) * [Blog](https://blocks.serp.co/blog) Customize Theme Toggle theme[Buy Pro!](https://blocks.serp.co/dashboard/billing) Toggle theme Customize Theme Toggle menu [Back to blog](https://blocks.serp.co/blog) Tailwind Long-Tail 10 min read Tailwind CSS Hero Section Best Tailwind CSS Hero Section Examples in 2026 =============================================== A comprehensive guide to hero section design patterns in Tailwind CSS — centered, split-screen, video, gradient, animated, and more. Featuring 81 ready-to-use hero blocks from SERP Blocks for React and Next.js. SB SERP Blocks Team Product Mar 21, 2026 ![Best Tailwind CSS Hero Section Examples in 2026 cover](https://blocks.serp.co/images/hero.png) The hero section is the most important piece of real estate on any webpage. It occupies the full viewport on load, it delivers your first impression, and it determines whether visitors scroll down or bounce. In 2026, the bar for hero section design is higher than ever — users expect polished typography, smooth animations, responsive behavior, and fast load times all at once. Tailwind CSS has become the dominant styling approach for building hero sections, and for good reason. Utility-first classes let you prototype and iterate on hero layouts in minutes rather than hours. You can fine-tune spacing, typography, and responsive behavior directly in your markup without context-switching to a separate stylesheet. This post covers the major hero section design patterns in Tailwind CSS, explains when each pattern works best, and shows how to approach layout, typography, and CTAs for maximum impact. We will reference examples from the [SERP Blocks hero collection](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/hero) , which includes 81 hero section blocks built with Tailwind CSS and Shadcn UI — but the design principles here apply to any Tailwind project. What Makes a Great Hero Section ------------------------------- Before looking at specific patterns, let us establish what every effective hero section needs: ### Visual Hierarchy The hero should have exactly three levels of content importance: 1. **The headline** — the largest, boldest text on the page. This is your one-sentence value proposition. Users should be able to read it in under two seconds. 2. **The supporting text** — a subheading or short paragraph that adds context to the headline. Smaller text, lighter weight, often in a muted color. 3. **The call to action** — one or two buttons that tell the user what to do next. These should be visually prominent and use action-oriented language ("Get Started," "Try Free," "See Pricing"). In Tailwind, this hierarchy translates directly to utility classes. Your headline might use `text-5xl font-bold tracking-tight` on desktop and `text-3xl` on mobile. Your supporting text drops to `text-lg text-muted-foreground`. Your CTA buttons use contrasting background colors and generous padding. ### Responsive Behavior A hero that looks great on a 27-inch monitor but breaks on a phone is a failed hero. Every layout decision needs a mobile-first consideration. In Tailwind, this means starting with the mobile layout and layering on responsive modifiers:
Split-screen layouts stack to single-column on mobile. Font sizes scale down. Padding adjusts. Background images shift or get replaced with simpler treatments. The best hero sections handle all of this gracefully. ### Performance Hero sections sit above the fold and directly impact your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) score — one of Google's Core Web Vitals. Heavy background images, unoptimized videos, and JavaScript-dependent animations can tank your LCP and hurt your search rankings. Use Next.js Image with `priority` for hero images. Lazy-load anything below the fold. Keep hero animations CSS-based rather than JavaScript-driven when possible. Prefer `backdrop-blur` and CSS gradients over image overlays. Hero Section Design Patterns ---------------------------- ### 1\. Centered Text Hero The workhorse of web design. A single column of centered text with a headline, subheading, and one or two CTA buttons. No images, no split layouts — just clean typography on a solid or gradient background. This pattern is effective because it focuses 100% of attention on your message. There is nothing to compete with the headline. It loads fast because there are no images. It is trivially responsive because a single column works at every breakpoint. In Tailwind, the structure looks like this:

Your headline here

Supporting description text

**When to use it:** SaaS landing pages, developer tools, API products, and any page where the message is more important than visuals. ### 2\. Split-Screen Hero The viewport divides into two halves — text content on one side, a visual (image, screenshot, illustration, or video) on the other. This is arguably the most versatile hero pattern because it communicates both a message and a visual simultaneously. The key Tailwind classes for a split-screen layout:
On mobile, the two halves stack vertically with text first. On desktop, they sit side by side. The `flex-1` class gives each side equal width, though you can adjust the ratio with `lg:w-3/5` and `lg:w-2/5` for asymmetric splits. **When to use it:** Product pages, app showcases, e-commerce homepages, and anywhere you want to show your product alongside the pitch. ### 3\. Hero with Full-Width Background Image A full-bleed background image spanning the entire viewport with text content overlaid. This creates a cinematic, immersive first impression that works well for visual brands. The challenge is readability. Text on images is inherently harder to read than text on solid backgrounds. The solution is overlay gradients:
The `bg-black/60` overlay ensures text remains readable regardless of what is happening in the background image. You can use gradient overlays (`bg-gradient-to-r from-black/80 to-transparent`) for a more sophisticated look that lets part of the image show through clearly. **When to use it:** Creative agencies, photography portfolios, travel and hospitality, real estate, and lifestyle brands. ### 4\. Gradient Background Hero Gradient backgrounds have become a signature look in 2026 tech and SaaS design. Linear gradients, radial gradients, mesh gradients, and aurora effects create visual interest without the performance cost of images. Tailwind makes simple gradients easy:
For more complex gradients — mesh gradients, animated aurora effects, or multi-stop radial patterns — you will need custom CSS or a utility plugin. The trend in 2026 leans toward subtle, low-contrast gradients that create depth without overwhelming the content. Think soft purple-to-blue transitions rather than aggressive rainbow gradients. **When to use it:** SaaS products, developer tools, fintech applications, and brands with strong color identities. ### 5\. Hero with Product Screenshot or Mockup A hero that features a large product screenshot, browser mockup, or device frame below or beside the headline. This is the "show, don't tell" approach — visitors see exactly what they are signing up for. The product image typically sits below the headline and CTA in a centered layout, or beside them in a split layout. Common treatments include: * Browser chrome frames around screenshots * Laptop or phone device mockups * Perspective transforms using `transform rotate-y-3` for a 3D angled look * Drop shadows with `shadow-2xl` for depth * Subtle float animations using CSS keyframes The SERP Blocks [hero collection](https://blocks.serp.co/blocks/hero) includes multiple variants of this pattern with different mockup styles and positioning options. **When to use it:** Any product with a visual interface — SaaS dashboards, design tools, mobile apps, and web applications. ### 6\. Hero with Social Proof Social proof built directly into the hero section — customer logos, testimonial quotes, rating stars, or user count badges. This pattern addresses the trust question immediately: "Are other people using this?" Common social proof elements in hero sections: * A row of customer or press logos below the CTA buttons * An avatar stack showing recent users ("Join 10,000+ developers") * A star rating with review count * A short testimonial quote from a recognizable name In Tailwind, a logo bar below the CTA might look like:
The `opacity-60 grayscale` treatment is a common technique that shows the logos without letting them visually overpower the hero content. On hover, you can remove these filters to reveal full-color logos. **When to use it:** Any product that has recognizable customers, press coverage, or strong user metrics to display. ### 7\. Video Background Hero Auto-playing, muted, looping video behind the hero text. This pattern creates immediate visual energy and is effective for brand storytelling, event pages, and creative portfolios.
Performance is the critical consideration. Video files are large. Use compressed MP4 (H.264), keep the video short (10-15 seconds), and provide a poster image that loads first. On mobile, consider replacing the video with a static image to save bandwidth. **When to use it:** Brand sites, event pages, media companies, and creative agencies. Use sparingly — video backgrounds can feel gimmicky if the content does not warrant them. ### 8\. Animated Hero with Motion Heroes that incorporate motion — text reveal animations, floating elements, particle effects, scroll-triggered transitions, or animated SVGs. These create a premium, polished feel when done well. In 2026, the trend is toward subtle, purposeful animation rather than flashy effects. A headline that fades up on load, a product screenshot that slides in from the right, or a gradient that slowly shifts colors — these feel modern without being distracting. Popular animation approaches with Tailwind: * CSS animations via Tailwind's `animate-` utilities (`animate-fade-in`, `animate-slide-up`) * Framer Motion for React-based entrance animations * CSS `@keyframes` for custom animations referenced with Tailwind's `animate-[custom]` syntax * `transition-all duration-500` for hover and interaction effects **When to use it:** Product launches, creative portfolios, and premium SaaS products. Avoid heavy animations on content-focused sites where they would distract from the message. ### 9\. Hero with Announcement Banner A hero section topped with a small banner or badge that highlights a recent announcement — "New: Version 3.0 released," "Featured on Product Hunt," or "Now with AI-powered search." The banner draws attention to news without changing the overall hero structure. The banner is typically a pill-shaped badge positioned above the headline: New Version 3.0 is now available **When to use it:** Products with active development cycles, SaaS tools with regular feature releases, and any product that wants to signal momentum. ### 10\. Minimal / Typography-Only Hero A stripped-down hero that relies entirely on typography — a large, bold headline with minimal or no supporting text, and sometimes no CTA button at all. The power comes from the words and the whitespace. This pattern is popular with agencies, portfolios, and brands that want to make a statement. It requires a strong headline because there is nothing else to carry the section. Typography choices matter more here than in any other pattern — font family, weight, letter spacing, and line height all contribute to the impact. **When to use it:** Agencies, creative portfolios, personal brand sites, and editorial publications. Typography Best Practices for Hero Sections ------------------------------------------- ### Headline Sizing The headline should be the largest text on the entire page. A common scale in Tailwind: * Mobile: `text-3xl` or `text-4xl` (30-36px) * Tablet: `sm:text-4xl` or `md:text-5xl` (36-48px) * Desktop: `lg:text-5xl` or `xl:text-6xl` (48-60px) Use `tracking-tight` (letter-spacing: -0.025em) on headlines to tighten the character spacing. Large text at default letter spacing looks loose and amateurish. Tight tracking makes headlines feel deliberate and polished. ### Line Length Keep headline lines under 15-20 words. Use `max-w-3xl` or `max-w-4xl` to constrain the text container so lines do not stretch across the full viewport on wide screens. Long lines are hard to read and make your hero look like a paragraph instead of a headline. ### Font Weight Headlines should be `font-bold` (700) or `font-extrabold` (800). The supporting text should be `font-normal` (400) or `font-medium` (500). This contrast in weight is what creates the visual hierarchy between headline and description. CTA Button Design ----------------- ### Primary and Secondary Actions Most hero sections benefit from two buttons: a primary action ("Get Started," "Try Free") and a secondary action ("Learn More," "Watch Demo"). The primary button uses a filled background (`bg-primary`), and the secondary uses an outline or ghost style (`border` or `bg-transparent`). This two-button pattern works because different visitors are at different stages. Someone ready to sign up clicks the primary CTA. Someone who needs more information clicks the secondary CTA. Both paths keep the visitor engaged. ### Button Size and Spacing Hero CTA buttons should be larger than standard buttons. Use `px-8 py-4 text-lg` rather than the default button sizing. The buttons need to be visually prominent from across the room — users should be able to spot the CTA instantly. Space buttons with `gap-4` in a flex container. On mobile, consider stacking buttons vertically with `flex-col sm:flex-row` so they do not get squeezed on narrow screens. Responsive Considerations ------------------------- ### Mobile-First Padding Start with generous mobile padding (`px-6 py-16`) and adjust for larger screens. It is better to have slightly too much padding on mobile than too little — cramped content on a small screen feels claustrophobic. ### Image Handling Background images should use `object-cover` to fill the viewport without distortion. On mobile, consider using a different image crop optimized for portrait orientation, or switch to a solid/gradient background when the image does not work at narrow widths. ### Minimum Height Use `min-h-[80vh]` or `min-h-screen` for hero sections to ensure they fill the viewport. What Makes a Great Hero Section ------------------------------- Before looking at specific patterns, let us establish what every effective hero section needs: ### Visual Hierarchy The hero should have exactly three levels of content importance: 1. **The headline** — the largest, boldest text on the page. This is your one-sentence value proposition. Users should be able to read it in under two seconds. 2. **The supporting text** — a subheading or short paragraph that adds context to the headline. Smaller text, lighter weight, often in a muted color. 3. **The call to action** — one or two buttons that tell the user what to do next. These should be visually prominent and use action-oriented language ("Get Started," "Try Free," "See Pricing"). In Tailwind, this hierarchy translates directly to utility classes. Your headline might use `text-5xl font-bold tracking-tight` on desktop and `text-3xl` on mobile. Your supporting text drops to `text-lg text-muted-foreground`. Your CTA buttons use contrasting background colors and generous padding. ### Responsive Behavior A hero that looks great on a 27-inch monitor but breaks on a phone is a failed hero. Every layout decision needs a mobile-first consideration. In Tailwind, this means starting with the mobile layout and layering on responsive modifiers:
Split-screen layouts stack to single-column on mobile. Font sizes scale down. Padding adjusts. Background images shift or get replaced with simpler treatments. The best hero sections handle all of this gracefully. ### Performance Hero sections sit above the fold and directly impact your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) score — one of Google's Core Web Vitals. Heavy background images, unoptimized videos, and JavaScript-dependent animations can tank your LCP and hurt your search rankings. Use Next.js Image with `priority` for hero images. Lazy-load anything below the fold. Keep hero animations CSS-based rather than JavaScript-driven when possible. Prefer `backdrop-blur` and CSS gradients over image overlays. Hero Section Design Patterns ---------------------------- ### 1\. Centered Text Hero The workhorse of web design. A single column of centered text with a headline, subheading, and one or two CTA buttons. No images, no split layouts — just clean typography on a solid or gradient background. This pattern is effective because it focuses 100% of attention on your message. There is nothing to compete with the headline. It loads fast because there are no images. It is trivially responsive because a single column works at every breakpoint. In Tailwind, the structure looks like this:

**When to use it:** SaaS landing pages, developer tools, API products, and any page where the message is more important than visuals. ### 2\. Split-Screen Hero The viewport divides into two halves — text content on one side, a visual (image, screenshot, illustration, or video) on the other. This is arguably the most versatile hero pattern because it communicates both a message and a visual simultaneously. The key Tailwind classes for a split-screen layout:
On mobile, the two halves stack vertically with text first. On desktop, they sit side by side. The `flex-1` class gives each side equal width, though you can adjust the ratio with `lg:w-3/5` and `lg:w-2/5` for asymmetric splits. **When to use it:** Product pages, app showcases, e-commerce homepages, and anywhere you want to show your product alongside the pitch. ### 3\. This creates a cinematic, immersive first impression that works well for visual brands. The challenge is readability. Text on images is inherently harder to read than text on solid backgrounds. The solution is overlay gradients:
The `bg-black/60` overlay ensures text remains readable regardless of what is happening in the background image. Gradient Background Hero Gradient backgrounds have become a signature look in 2026 tech and SaaS design. Linear gradients, radial gradients, mesh gradients, and aurora effects create visual interest without the performance cost of images. Tailwind makes simple gradients easy:

This is the "show, don't tell" approach — visitors see exactly what they are signing up for. The product image typically sits below the headline and CTA in a centered layout, or beside them in a split layout. Hero with Social Proof Social proof built directly into the hero section — customer logos, testimonial quotes, rating stars, or user count badges. This pattern addresses the trust question immediately: "Are other people using this?" Common social proof elements in hero sections: * A row of customer or press logos below the CTA buttons * An avatar stack showing recent users ("Join 10,000+ developers") * A star rating with review count * A short testimonial quote from a recognizable name In Tailwind, a logo bar below the CTA might look like:
The `opacity-60 grayscale` treatment is a common technique that shows the logos without letting them visually overpower the hero content. On hover, you can remove these filters to reveal full-color logos. **When to use it:** Any product that has recognizable customers, press coverage, or strong user metrics to display. ### 7\. Video Background Hero Auto-playing, muted, looping video behind the hero text. This pattern creates immediate visual energy and is effective for brand storytelling, event pages, and creative portfolios.
Performance is the critical consideration. Video files are large. Use compressed MP4 (H.264), keep the video short (10-15 seconds), and provide a poster image that loads first. On mobile, consider replacing the video with a static image to save bandwidth. **When to use it:** Brand sites, event pages, media companies, and creative agencies. Use sparingly — video backgrounds can feel gimmicky if the content does not warrant them. ### 8\. Animated Hero with Motion Heroes that incorporate motion — text reveal animations, floating elements, particle effects, scroll-triggered transitions, or animated SVGs. These create a premium, polished feel when done well. In 2026, the trend is toward subtle, purposeful animation rather than flashy effects. A headline that fades up on load, a product screenshot that slides in from the right, or a gradient that slowly shifts colors — these feel modern without being distracting. Popular animation approaches with Tailwind: * CSS animations via Tailwind's `animate-` utilities (`animate-fade-in`, `animate-slide-up`) * Framer Motion for React-based entrance animations * CSS `@keyframes` for custom animations referenced with Tailwind's `animate-[custom]` syntax * `transition-all duration-500` for hover and interaction effects **When to use it:** Product launches, creative portfolios, and premium SaaS products. Avoid heavy animations on content-focused sites where they would distract from the message. ### 9\. Hero with Announcement Banner A hero section topped with a small banner or badge that highlights a recent announcement — "New: Version 3.0 released," "Featured on Product Hunt," or "Now with AI-powered search." The banner draws attention to news without changing the overall hero structure. The banner is typically a pill-shaped badge positioned above the headline: New Version 3.0 is now available **When to use it:** Products with active development cycles, SaaS tools with regular feature releases, and any product that wants to signal momentum. ### 10\. Minimal / Typography-Only Hero A stripped-down hero that relies entirely on typography — a large, bold headline with minimal or no supporting text, and sometimes no CTA button at all. The power comes from the words and the whitespace. This pattern is popular with agencies, portfolios, and brands that want to make a statement. It requires a strong headline because there is nothing else to carry the section. Typography choices matter more here than in any other pattern — font family, weight, letter spacing, and line height all contribute to the impact. **When to use it:** Agencies, creative portfolios, personal brand sites, and editorial publications. Typography Best Practices for Hero Sections ------------------------------------------- ### Headline Sizing The headline should be the largest text on the entire page. A common scale in Tailwind: * Mobile: `text-3xl` or `text-4xl` (30-36px) * Tablet: `sm:text-4xl` or `md:text-5xl` (36-48px) * Desktop: `lg:text-5xl` or `xl:text-6xl` (48-60px) Use `tracking-tight` (letter-spacing: -0.025em) on headlines to tighten the character spacing. Large text at default letter spacing looks loose and amateurish. Tight tracking makes headlines feel deliberate and polished. ### Line Length Keep headline lines under 15-20 words. Use `max-w-3xl` or `max-w-4xl` to constrain the text container so lines do not stretch across the full viewport on wide screens. Long lines are hard to read and make your hero look like a paragraph instead of a headline. ### Font Weight Headlines should be `font-bold` (700) or `font-extrabold` (800). The supporting text should be `font-normal` (400) or `font-medium` (500). This contrast in weight is what creates the visual hierarchy between headline and description. The primary button uses a filled background (`bg-primary`), and the secondary uses an outline or ghost style (`border` or `bg-transparent`). This two-button pattern works because different visitors are at different stages. Someone ready to sign up clicks the primary CTA. Someone who needs more information clicks the secondary CTA. Both paths keep the visitor engaged. ### Button Size and Spacing Hero CTA buttons should be larger than standard buttons. Use `px-8 py-4 text-lg` rather than the default button sizing. The buttons need to be visually prominent from across the room — users should be able to spot the CTA instantly. Space buttons with `gap-4` in a flex container. On mobile, consider stacking buttons vertically with `flex-col sm:flex-row` so they do not get squeezed on narrow screens.
